performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: The clarinet sings a D major melody, and the orchestra answers in phrases of its own. William McColl plays the Adagio on a basset clarinet he built himself, with Abraham Kaplan and the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: A · Clarinet above gently moving strings
sections.mNote: A D major melody with room to breathe

sections.label: A′ · The orchestra answers the singer
sections.mNote: Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings’ reply

relations.label: The orchestra answers the solo melody
relations.basis: The first A section sets the clarinet’s opening phrase against an orchestral answer near 34 s. The melodic material is shared, but its scoring changes. These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The opening melody returns
relations.basis: After the contrasting middle, the A′ section restores the solo melody. The matched later excerpt falls inside the return marked near 262 s, not at a claimed precise entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.953, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 266.5 s (cache/form/mozart-clarinet-adagio.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A song without words
cues.text: The clarinet begins over gently moving violins and held viola notes. Cellos provide a light bass; double basses and the orchestral winds wait. The melody rises, lingers and falls, with rests that give each phrase a singer’s breath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, p. 236: solo clarinet, violins, viola and cello; double basses and winds rest. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f7/IMSLP29515-PMLP03144-Mozart_Clarinet_Concerto_K622.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra answers in D
cues.text: The orchestra answers the solo phrase. Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings, and the double basses add weight beneath them. The melody belongs to the violins now, with the clarinet doubling their line in the printed score.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, first tutti, p. 236. The edition prints the solo clarinet doubling the violin melody during tutti passages.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: McColl builds his clarinet
cues.text: William McColl plays an instrument of his own construction in this December 1987 performance. The basset clarinet extends the ordinary clarinet’s low range, giving Mozart’s soloist more room beneath the stave.
cues.evidence: The Soni Ventorum archive identifies McColl’s self-built basset clarinet and the December 1987 performance: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html. The extended low range is described by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

cues.title: The singer grows more elaborate
cues.text: The middle section begins in A major. The clarinet decorates its line with quick runs and wider leaps, while the strings accompany softly. Long notes and little flurries alternate, like a singer finding more to say between breaths.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 237–238. Calvin Dotsey describes the more ornamental central section: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An audience falls quiet
cues.text: On 7 October 1791, while finishing the concerto, Mozart writes to Constanze in Baden after another full house for The Magic Flute. What pleases him most is its “silent applause”: the audience’s absorbed attention during the music.
cues.evidence: Mozart to Constanze, Vienna, 7–8 October 1791, Bauer–Deutsch 1193: “was mich aber am meisten freuet, ist, der Stille beifall!” He also reports orchestrating the concerto’s rondo. Our translation: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1193.pdf.

cues.title: The first melody returns
cues.text: A pause on the dominant prepares the return of the D major melody. The clarinet resumes over the softly moving strings; the double basses fall silent again. Mozart shortens the return, then lets the soloist add a more ornate closing passage.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 239–241: dominant fermata, return and coda. The shortened reprise is described by Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A last decorated phrase
cues.text: The clarinet adds curling figures and a trill above quiet strings. The melody stays close to D major as the phrases settle. Winds and horns return for the closing cadence, placing a soft orchestral frame around the soloist’s last notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, coda, p. 241.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violins take up the song
transitions.from: A · Clarinet above gently moving strings
transitions.to: A′ · The orchestra answers the singer
transitions.how: The solo phrase closes on A, the dominant of D major. Moving string notes lead into the orchestral answer in D. Flutes, bassoons, horns and double basses join, while the violins take the melody over the continuing accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, first solo and tutti, p. 236.

transitions.title: A major and a freer solo
transitions.from: A′ · The orchestra answers the singer
transitions.how: The orchestral reply closes and the winds fall silent. The clarinet begins the A major middle section above soft strings, extending its phrases into runs and leaps. The accompaniment keeps the slow three-beat measure beneath these quicker notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 237–238.

transitions.title: A pause on A, then D
transitions.to: A″ · The D major melody returns
transitions.how: Orchestral chords alternate with clarinet runs, leading to a fermata on A major, the dominant. After the pause, the opening tune returns in D over the violins’ flowing accompaniment. Winds and double basses rest, restoring the light scoring of the beginning.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, p. 239.

transitions.title: The winds leave the closing solo
transitions.to: Coda · One more solo in D
transitions.how: The orchestral reply reaches D major, and the winds fall silent. A rising clarinet figure begins the coda over quiet strings. The soloist ornaments the closing phrases before winds and horns return for the final D major cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 240–241.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto in A, K. 622, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke Serie XII No. 20, 1881, plate W.A.M. 622)
source.locator: II. Adagio, printed pp. 236–241: solo phrases, orchestral answers and coda. The double basses rest beneath the opening solo and its return.

Wind chords alternate with clarinet runs, leading to a fermata.
The opening melody returns over strings; double basses and winds rest.
Flutes, bassoons and horns join the violins’ fuller reply.
The clarinet decorates the coda above soft strings; double basses rejoin near the close.
Flutes, bassoons and horns return for the soft D major cadence.

quote.text: In an opera, poetry must simply be music’s obedient daughter.
quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
